new_statements.citation: Lipp, Timothy. 2014. A Sociolinguistic Study of Western Tamang in Nepal. Kathmandu: Linguistic Survey of Nepal (LinSuN), Central Department of Linguistics, Tribhuvan University & SIL International. 66-page report (+ 99 pp. appendices, separate file, not downloaded). SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 59839.
new_statements.locator: Section 1.3.1 'Language description', printed p. 6 (p. 16 of 67); text in line 454
new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.relation_note: One sentence: 'Western Tamang.. is tonal (Eppele et al. 2012)' in the background section. The rest of the report is sociolinguistic (wordlist lexical similarity, RTT comprehension, dialect mapping, vitality); the 'more divergent linguistic traits' of tge in the abstract are cashed out in sec. 8.1 as 'differing ethnic identity, and slightly lower lexical similarity', not phonology.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The report states only, secondhand from Ethnologue Nepal (Eppele, Regmi & Yadava 2012), that Western Tamang is tonal; it gives no description of the tone system and says nothing about word stress. No variety-specific prosodic remark for Eastern Gorkha Tamang [tge] appears anywhere in the 66 pages (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text for stress/tone/tonal/pitch/accent/prosod: this one hit only).
new_statements.identity_note: The survey's scope explicitly includes Eastern Gorkha Tamang [tge] (Kashigaun VDC, Gorkha; fieldwork January 2014) alongside [tdg] and [tmk]; the tonal sentence is about 'Western Tamang' as the Ethnologue grouping that then contained tge, cited from Ethnologue, not an observation made at the tge site.

tone_statements.citation: Varenkamp, Bryan. 1996. Tamang tam: a sociolinguistic study of Eastern Tamang dialects (in Nepal). Kirtipur: CNAS, Tribhuvan University. xx+135 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Along with all the other languages in the “Tamang sub-family” or Gurung Branch, Tamang is tonal, albeit “semi-tonal or marginally tonal” (Mazaudon 1978:157). The tone in Tamang is not like that of Chinese, in which each syllable has a distinct tone; rather, the tones of the Tamang sub-group languages spread across the whole word. [...] Most contemporary scholars recognize that Tamang exhibits four tones. However, tone is not distinctive in and of itself. It is part of a complex bundle of three elements: 1) voiced versus unvoiced consonants, 2) breathy or lax versus non-breathy or tense vowel quality, and 3) level or contour (falling or rising) pitch.
tone_statements.locator: Chapter 'The Tamang language', section 'Tone', p. 25 (continuing on p. 26)
tone_statements.summary: Group-level (Tamang / Tamangic as a whole, secondhand after Mazaudon 1978): four lexical word-tones whose domain is the whole word, each a bundle of pitch height/contour, onset voicing and breathy vs clear phonation ('marginally tonal'); no variety-specific statement for Kashigaun/Kerauja and no tone marking in the tge word list.
